Information Security Policy Overview: The Basics
RealPage is in the business of trust. Our clients trust us to protect the confidentiality and security of their data.
Our clients’ consumers trust us to protect the privacy and security of their personal information. Therefore,
every RealPage employee is responsible for understanding and following procedures that reduce risk to our
Company, our clients and their consumers.

Each employee serves as the first line of defense in managing those risks by protecting RealPage’s information
systems, products and other assets. You are responsible for understanding information security principles, the
operational risks associated with your role and managing those risks appropriately.

The requirements documented in this section describe three key principles that help maintain security of
sensitive information and data. Employees are expected to comply with the key principles at all times.

These principles are as follows:

    •   Act in ways that protect sensitive Company data, client data and consumer information

    •   Use RealPage’s assets for business purposes only

    •   Use RealPage’s communication systems in an appropriate and safe manner

This overview should not be considered comprehensive. RealPage expects employees to use sound judgment
and to act in ways that protect RealPage’s information, assets and communication systems. If you have
questions, you should work with your manager and the RealPage IT Security team to ensure that your actions
comply with the RealPage Information Security Policy.

Failure to act in ways that protect RealPage’s information, assets, and communication systems or failure
to cooperate with inquiries or investigations may result in corrective action, including termination of your
employment. Every employee is required to report anything that may violate the Information Security Policy
or place the Company’s information, assets and communication systems at risk. In the event of a suspected
or potential security incident, you should err on the side of caution and report the situation to the Security
Incident Response Team. Methods for reporting such situations are outlined within this section.

Appropriate use of RealPage systems, products and services
The use of RealPage’s information technology systems, products and services is a privilege granted to each
employee based on roles and responsibilities. These systems give employees the ability to deliver service
and communicate with clients, business partners and other employees in a secure and reliable manner while
minimizing risk and maintaining compliance with regulatory and legal standards.

To mitigate risk, employees are required to use electronic communication, system features, and content
appropriately and in accordance with established requirements and business procedures. RealPage systems,
products and services may be used for business purposes only; personal use is strictly prohibited.

                                                                                                            82

The following are examples of prohibited activities:

    •      Using system access and RealPage login credentials for personal reasons, such as accessing a client’s
           database to view your own (or someone else’s) lease application, rent ledger, resident profile, or other
           data owned and controlled by a client

    •      Hacking or otherwise attempting to gain unauthorized access to systems, products or resources,
           including attempts to disrupt service

    •      Posting/storing proprietary content or sensitive data in unapproved or personal websites, blogs, chat
           rooms, mobile applications or other social media applications

    •      Downloading or forwarding chain letters, viruses, or attachments from unknown or suspicious third
           parties

    •      Downloading and/or installing pirated software or other electronic files on RealPage systems or hardware

    •      Transmitting, retrieving or storing any communications of a defamatory, discriminatory, harassing or
           pornographic nature

Under no circumstances are employees allowed to use RealPage information technology systems in a way that
could violate the Company’s policies or any federal, state, or local regulations.

Monitoring of Company systems and equipment
RealPage will monitor and may control access to and use of its equipment and information technology systems,
including but not limited to: original and backup copies of email, instant messaging, text messaging, voicemail
and Internet use. You should not expect privacy in connection with your use of any Company resources,
equipment or property. Even if data is encrypted and you have created or have access to passwords to protect
against unauthorized access, you should not consider activities or correspondence using that password to be
private.

All telephone and email transmissions or conversations, or any internet access or usage, via the use of any

means. In addition, phone calls made or received on any business telephone may be monitored or recorded.
Monitoring may be conducted remotely or locally using software, hardware or other means. Information
obtained through monitoring may be shared with management, Human Resources and IT security. It will be
treated confidentially and retained for a reasonable period to accomplish the purpose for which it was collected
as determined by RealPage, and it is subject to any rights employees may have under applicable law.

If you have questions or concerns about the appropriate use of RealPage systems or equipment, contact your
supervisor or IT Security.

Protecting RealPage information
Confidential information and intellectual property, including trade secrets, are extremely valuable to RealPage,
clients and consumers. Treat them accordingly and do not jeopardize them through your business or personal
use of electronic communications systems, including email, text messaging, Internet access, social media,
telephone conversations, and/or voice mail. Disclosure of the Company’s confidential information to anyone
outside RealPage and use of the Company’s intellectual property is strictly prohibited without authorization
from the RealPage Legal Department. Ask your supervisor if you are unsure whether to disclose confidential
information to specific individuals or how to safeguard the Company’s proprietary rights.

This policy also prohibits use of the Company’s IT resources and communications systems in any manner that
would infringe or violate the proprietary rights of third parties. Electronic communications systems provide
easy access to vast amounts of information, including material that is protected by copyright, trademark,
patent, and/or trade secret law. You should not knowingly use or distribute for business purposes any such
material downloaded from the Internet or received by email without the prior written permission of the
RealPage Legal Department.

Information access and sharing - “need to know”
Every RealPage employee’s access to Company resources and information is considered a privilege. An
appropriate level of information access is granted to employees according to their business role and need.

Employees may receive proprietary information relating to RealPage and client operations in the course of their
work and are obligated to protect such information from disclosure. Employees must disclose information only
to authorized parties who have a business need to know. Company and consumer information may be disclosed
only within RealPage or to nonaffiliated parties in accordance with applicable law, confidentiality agreements,
and privacy policies. It is your responsibility to ensure that the request for information meets
these requirements.

If you’re not sure whether information should be shared with or disclosed to another party, ask your supervisor or
IT Security.

Sensitive information (data) handling
“Sensitive information” (or data) refers to confidential, privileged or proprietary information that is not available
to or readily accessible by the general public. If sensitive information is lost or used in any way other than
intended, the result can be severe damage to the people or organization to which that information belongs.

Common examples of sensitive information include:

    •   Personally Identifiable Information (PII): Social Security numbers, DOB, driver’s license numbers,
        financial account information, medical records

    •   Company trade secrets, documents, emails marked “privileged and confidential,” corporate financial
        documents and account information

                                                                                                            84

All sensitive RealPage data (Company data, client data and consumer personal information) must be handled
appropriately and protected from unauthorized access or misuse. This requirement always exists, including
during storage, transmission, usage and even disposal. Therefore, all RealPage employees must adhere to the
following best practices:

    •   Do not access sensitive information unless there is a valid business purpose for doing so. Any access of
        sensitive information for personal reasons is strictly prohibited.

    •   Do not communicate or otherwise transfer sensitive information to others unless you know they are
        approved or authorized to receive it.

    •   Do not store unencrypted sensitive information on a laptop computer/desktop computer’s hard drive,
        USB drive, CD, flash memory card, floppy drive or other storage media. Do not store unencrypted
        sensitive information on any smartphone, tablet or other mobile computing device.

    •   Do not transmit sensitive information via any wireless technology, email or the Internet unless the
        connection is secure, or the information is encrypted.

    •   Do not store sensitive information obtained from RealPage systems on third- party media or other systems
        (Dropbox, Amazon Cloud, Apple iCloud, etc.) unless doing so in accordance with business unit procedures
        or explicitly authorized by RealPage IT Security.

    •   Dispose of media (disks, tapes, hard drives, etc.) that contain confidential information in a manner that
        protects the confidentiality of the information.

Workstation security
Every RealPage employee must protect sensitive information by ensuring proper control of access into any
business-related work area and ensuring vigilant housekeeping practices, such as shredding or other secure
document disposal.

Usernames & passwords
Safeguard all types of personal authenticators to prevent unauthorized use by others by following these best
practices:

    •   Authorization or access to certain systems and information within RealPage or external vendor systems
        is granted based upon confirmation of your username and password. Protect your passwords, just as
        you would protect other types of restricted information:

         – Do not disclose, display or share passwords with anyone, including your manager

         – Do not request an employee, client, or consumer’s username or password to access accounts

         – Change your password immediately and notify IT Security if you suspect that it has been
             compromised

                                                                                                         85

Securing your devices
Always keep your laptop, other mobile computing devices (smartphones/tablets), and portable digital storage
media safe and secure by adhering to the following best practices:

    •   Never leave your computer unattended without first shutting it down or locking your screen (press
        CTRL+ALT+DELETE then ENTER).

    •   At the end of the day, if you do not take your laptop or other mobile devices home, store them in a locked
        drawer or file cabinet.

    •   When traveling, take extra precaution to protect your equipment and its information:

         – Power down the laptop completely by selecting Shut Down after pressing CTRL+ALT+DELETE
            or from the Start menu before you transport the laptop

         – Never check laptops as luggage; always keep your laptop with you

         – Whenever possible, lock your mobile devices and media in the hotel room safe

    •   Never leave your laptop in an unlocked car or in a car overnight.

    •   When attending offsite meetings, do not leave your laptop unattended.

    •   When working from home, do not let family members or anyone else use your work computer or any other
        mobile computing devices or portable digital storage media. Under no circumstances are unauthorized
        parties allowed to use RealPage devices.

Protecting RealPage hardware & software assets
RealPage computing hardware and software (“assets”) are Company property and provided for use to
facilitate Company business. Assets issued to employees are an extension of the office and must be secured in
accordance with RealPage policies and procedures. Employees are responsible for protecting assets from loss,
theft and damage while they are in the employee’s possession. Under no circumstances are employees allowed
to use RealPage assets in a way that could violate RealPage policies. RealPage reserves the right to monitor any
Company assets to ensure compliance with these policies and to maintain legal and regulatory standards.

RealPage IT systems & software
All software installed or developed on RealPage IT systems, and any data collected, downloaded or created via
these systems is the exclusive property of RealPage.

Employees may not copy or transmit RealPage data outside the Company without a predefined business need,
and then only in an authorized manner. Upon termination of employment, no employee shall remove, copy, or
destroy such software or data from Company systems.

                                                                                                        86

RealPage-issued mobile devices
RealPage may issue employees Company-owned smartphones, mobile phones or tablets for the purpose of
conducting RealPage business. Security software installed on mobile computing devices must not be disabled or
removed under any circumstances. Even with security software in place, employees must immediately report a
lost, stolen or confiscated mobile computing device to IT Security.

Reporting security incidents
Any RealPage employee who believes that an information security incident has occurred must report
it immediately. This helps to contain the incident and assists with managing its impact. Under certain
circumstances, RealPage may be required to notify clients, consumers and others if sensitive information is
compromised.

Some examples of information security incidents include:

    •   Unauthorized or improper use, attempted use, or access to RealPage information technology systems
        and products

    •   Loss, theft or confiscation of a RealPage computer or mobile device

    •   Discovery of product or system vulnerabilities, malfunctions or other errors

    •   Misappropriation or unauthorized use of RealPage employee access credentials (badges) and
        authentication (usernames/passwords)

To report a security incident: contact the Security Incident Response Team at: SIRT@realpage.com or
972-820-4745

Email Usage
Created as a business tool to help employees serve customers, communicate with suppliers, streamline internal
communications and reduce unnecessary paperwork, the email system is intended primarily for business
purposes. Employees accessing the Company’s email system are required to adhere to the following policies
and procedures. Violation of the Company’s email policy may result in disciplinary action, up to and including
termination.

    1. All communications and information transmitted, received, or archived in the Company’s computer
        system belong to the Company and are subject to audit at any time. The law gives Company
        management the right to access and disclose all employee email messages transmitted or received via
        the Company’s computer system. Employees should have no expectation of privacy when using the
        Company email system. The Company may exercise its legal right to monitor employees’ email activity.
        Be aware that management may access and monitor email at any time for any reason without notice.

                                                                                                         87

2. The email system is reserved primarily for business use. Employee’s nominal use of the Company’s email
     system for personal reasons is allowed provided it does not affect productivity.

3. Privacy is difficult if not impossible to achieve in the electronic age. Confidential or personal information
     should never be sent via email without the understanding that it can be intercepted. This includes the
     transmission of customer financial information, Social Security numbers, employee health records,
     proprietary data and trade secrets, and/or other confidential material. When sending confidential
     material (or any messages), employees should use extreme caution to ensure that the intended
     recipient’s email address is correct.

4. Exercise sound judgment and common sense when distributing email messages. Client-related messages
     should be carefully guarded and protected, like any other written materials. You must also abide by
     copyright laws, ethics rules and other applicable laws. Exercise caution when using the “Reply to All”
     feature of Outlook or sending blind carbon copies to ensure that you don’t violate addressees’ privacy
     by inadvertently sending carbon copies.

5. Email usage must conform to the Company’s harassment and discrimination policies. Messages
     containing libelous, defamatory, obscene, menacing, threatening, offensive, harassing, or otherwise
     objectionable and/or inappropriate statements — and/or messages that disclose personal information
     without authorization — are prohibited. If you receive this type of prohibited, unsolicited message, do
     not forward it. Notify your manager or the Human Resources department about the message. Handle
     the message as instructed by management.

6. Email messages should be treated as formal business documents, written in accordance with the
     Company’s guidelines. Style, spelling, grammar and punctuation should be appropriate and accurate,
     and the rules of etiquette must be observed. Auto forwarding of email to vendors, clients, or parties
     outside the Company is forbidden. The content and tone of the emails must reflect the official
     responsibilities of the author. Remember that it may be exposed to public scrutiny if it is demanded in a
     legal discovery process.

7.   Employees are prohibited from sending Company-wide email messages to all employees unless
     doing so is part of their regular job duties. Only a designated member of the Information Technology
     organization and/or systems administrator may generate public mail distribution lists.

8. Employees should not waste the Company’s computer resources or colleague’s time. Send email
     messages and copies only to those with a legitimate need to read your message. Chain messages and
     executable graphics should be deleted, not forwarded, as they can overload the system.

9.   Employees are responsible for knowing and adhering to the Company’s email retention and
     deletion policies.

                                                                                                      88

C O M M U N I C AT I O N S

                             89

RealPage Communications Policy
The way RealPage and its employees conduct communications across various public forums can have a
profound impact on how the Company is portrayed by outside parties, influencing both our corporate
reputation and the perception among our current and prospective clients, employees, investors, analysts, media
and competitors. This policy details guidelines for RealPage employees in their use of social media, media, and
corporate and public communications.

Confidential and proprietary information
RealPage employees and other Company representatives must maintain the confidentiality of information
considered by RealPage to be confidential, including Company data, customer data, partner and/or supplier
data, personal employee data, and any information not generally available to the public.

Disclosure of Company information
You must not comment or communicate any confidential RealPage information, such as RealPage’s clients,
investors, or past or future business performance, business plans, or prospects. This includes statements
regarding:

    •   Confidential or financial information

    •   Product development

    •   Business strategy

    •   Trade secrets, including competitors

    •   Current legal procedures

    •   Personal information

The following policy and guidelines cover all forms of public communications, including but not limited to the
following:

    •   Communications on behalf of RealPage

    •   Online, print and broadcast media inquiries

    •   Legal inquiries

    •   Social media, multimedia, networking, blogs and self-published content

All RealPage employees and Company representatives may not knowingly communicate information that is
untrue or deceptive. RealPage will take all reasonable steps to assure the validity of information communicated
via any channel, but it is the responsibility of the Company representative to ensure accuracy in the first
instance.

                                                                                                          90

Use of the Company name
Unless prior authorization in writing signed by an officer of the Company has been received or contacts with
the press are an expected aspect of your job duties, no employee may use the Company name to give the
impression that they are acting on behalf of the Company. The Company name includes any logos and/or
designs that are commonly used by the Company.

    I.   Communication on behalf of RealPage
         Only the Senior Vice President, Communications, the Director of Investor Relations and executive
         officers of the Company are authorized to make statements in any forum on behalf of the Company.
         No other employees may communicate on behalf of the Company without express permission from the
         Senior Vice President, Communications, the Director of Investor Relations or an executive officer of
         the Company.

    II. Online, print, and broadcast media inquiries
         All press inquiries, including online, print or broadcast media seeking official RealPage information or
         statements, must be routed through the Senior Vice President, Communications. This department is
         responsible for corporate fact checking, coordinating executive briefs or interviews, and handling direct
         inquiries. Do not engage in open dialogue or answer questions about any specific topic on behalf of the
         Company. Direct all such media inquiries to corporate.communications@realpage.com.

    III. Responding to inquiries submitted via social media
         From time to time, employees using social media for official business or personal purposes may receive
         inquiries or contact related to RealPage operations. Any employee receiving such contact should refrain
         from responding or engaging in open dialogue on behalf of RealPage and direct the contact to the
         RealPage Marketing Department at socialmedia@realpage.com for handling.

         If you are unsure about any particular communication or posting, please contact RealPage Marketing at
         socialmedia@realpage.com for further clarification.

    IV. Legal inquiries
         If you receive a subpoena, correspondence or request for information from any federal, state, or local
         governmental agency that is directed to RealPage or to you in your capacity as a supervisor or manager
         of RealPage, you must immediately notify the RealPage Legal Department at legal@realpage.com and
         direct all such legal inquiries to the Legal Department.

                                                                                                           91

Social and Digital Media Policies
Conduct on social media
At RealPage, we understand that social media can be a fun and rewarding way to share your life and opinions
with family, friends, clients and fellow employees around the world. Digital and social media channels also
allow us to promote RealPage products and services to a mass audience, while engaging individuals through
conversation and knowledge exchange.

Participating in social media also has the potential to affect our Company reputation and expose RealPage to
business and legal risks. To manage these risks effectively, all RealPage employees need to know, understand
and put into practice the guidelines for acceptable use of social media. This policy applies to all RealPage
employees and members of the Company’s Board of Directors in their capacity as representatives of RealPage.
This policy also applies to third-party agents and contractors who act on behalf of RealPage.

Using social media for personal use
We encourage you to use social media to gain and share information about RealPage. However, it is important to
remember that as an employee, you are perceived by members of the public as a representative of RealPage when
participating in personal and business communications. This applies even if you include a statement in your profile
that your opinions are your own.

Digital and social media channels include all means of communicating or posting information or content of any
sort (for business and personal use) on the Internet, including to your own or someone else’s web log or blog,
journal or diary, personal web site, video sharing site, wiki, social networking or affinity web site, web bulletin
board, consumer review site, or a chat room, whether or not associated or affiliated with RealPage, as well as
any other form of electronic communication.

You are solely responsible for what you post online. Before creating online content or posts, consider some of the
risks and rewards that are involved. Keep in mind that any conduct that adversely affects your job performance or
the performance of fellow associates, or that otherwise adversely affects members, customers, suppliers, people
who work on behalf of RealPage or RealPage’s legitimate business interests, may result in disciplinary action up to
and including termination.

Carefully read and follow these policies. Inappropriate postings that may include discriminatory remarks,
harassment, and threats of violence or similar inappropriate or unlawful conduct will not be tolerated and may
subject you to disciplinary action up to and including termination.

                                                                                                            92

Do’s:
1. Be fair and courteous to fellow employees, clients, vendors, independent contractors or any other person
    who works on behalf of RealPage.

2. Be honest and accurate when posting information or news, and if you make a mistake, correct it quickly.

3. Maintain the confidentiality of RealPage trade secrets, private or confidential information and financial
    discourse laws. Trade secrets may include information regarding the development of systems, processes,
    products, know-how and technology.

4. Be cognizant of the content, your neighbors, and workspace (such as appearance of proprietary information)
    when shooting amateur video content at or during a RealPage office or affiliated property. Please use your
    best judgment in displaying this information out of context, and/or without prior approval from those in
    the video.

5. Express only your personal opinions. Never represent yourself as a spokesperson for RealPage.

6. Refrain from using digital or social media while on work time or on equipment provided by RealPage unless
    it is work related as authorized by your manager.

Don’ts:
1. Avoid using statements, photographs, video or audio that reasonably could be viewed as malicious, obscene,
    threatening or intimidating, that disparage customers, employees or suppliers, or that might constitute
    harassment or bullying.

2. Never post any information that you know to be false about RealPage fellow employees, clients, vendors,
    independent contractors or any other person affiliated with RealPage.

3. Do not post internal reports, policies, procedures or other internal business-related confidential
    communications. It is illegal to communicate or give a “tip” on inside information to others so that they may
    buy or sell stocks or securities.

4. Do not post any personal video content that includes the names of RealPage brands, partners or customers
    to video sharing sites (including but not limited to YouTube) without approval from the RealPage Marketing
    department. To inquire about approval, please contact socialmedia@realpage.com.

5. Do not use RealPage email addresses to register on social networks, blogs, video sites or other online tools
    utilized for personal use.

                                                                                                        93

RealPage prohibits taking negative action against any employee for reporting a possible deviation from
this policy or for cooperating in an investigation. Any employee who retaliates against another employee
for reporting a possible deviation from this policy or for cooperating in an investigation will be subject to
disciplinary action, up to and including termination.

Employee use of social media on behalf of RealPage
    •   Creation & approval: No official RealPage website, digital or social media channel, account, or platform
        can exist or be created without prior permission from the RealPage Marketing department. This
        restriction includes social media accounts created for product testing purposes. Please route such
        requests through RealPage’s Marketing Department at socialmedia@realpage.com.

    •   Branding & logos: All official RealPage digital and social media accounts and platforms must adhere to
        the requirements of the RealPage Brand Center located at https://www.realpage.com/brand/.

    •   Company & product descriptions: All official RealPage digital and social media channels, websites,
        accounts, and platforms must have current Marketing-approved Company descriptions, product and
        services information, and imagery.

    •   Usernames & passwords: Employees responsible for managing official RealPage digital and social media
        channels, websites, accounts, and platforms must provide up-to-date log in, password and access
        information for each asset to RealPage’s Marketing Department at socialmedia@realpage.com. All
        passwords must be changed every quarter (90 days).

    •   Content: All content posted to digital and social media channels, websites, accounts, and platforms must
        be completely accurate and not deceptive or misleading. Employees responsible for managing official
        RealPage digital and social media properties are prohibited from disclosing confidential or proprietary
        information concerning RealPage operations, including but not limited to: nonpublic financial and
        operations data, mergers and acquisition activity, and product development projects. Employees are
        likewise prohibited from utilizing or creating posts that include confidential or copyrighted information
        (music, videos, text, etc.) belonging to third parties.

    •   Removal of content: RealPage may elect, at any time, to remove content from official RealPage social
        and digital media channels, websites, accounts, and platforms to maintain compliance with applicable
        laws, regulations or legal requests. RealPage likewise reserves the right to remove or request removal
        of any posted employee or third-party content that is inappropriate for the topic discussed, uses
        inappropriate or offensive language, or violates the corporate privacy policy.

If you have questions, please contact socialmedia@realpage.com.

                                                                                                           94

Conduct on Internal Communications Channels
The same policies in place for social media also apply to internal channels, including email messages,
conversations on Microsoft Teams, posts on Viva Engage/Yammer or via another internal communication
channel including, but not limited to Seismic, Slack, etc.

As with external channels, RealPage reserves the right to remove or request removal of any posted content
that is inappropriate for the topic discussed, uses inappropriate or offensive language, or violates the corporate
privacy policy.

If you have questions or concerns about a message or communications, please contact the Communications
team at corporate.communications@realpage.com.

Solicitations, Distributions and Posting of Materials
RealPage prohibits the solicitation, distribution and posting of materials on or at Company premises by any
employee or non-employee, except as outlined below. Company premises means property owned, leased,
operated, managed or controlled by RealPage, including buildings, parking lots and other areas that RealPage
has the right to use exclusively or in common with others. RealPage’s property does not include public premises,
such as public streets and public sidewalks.

Provisions:
    •   Employees may not distribute literature of any kind during work times, except in connection with a
        Company-sponsored event.

    •   Employees may only admit non-employees to Company premises with management approval or as
        part of a Company-sponsored program. These visits should not disrupt workflow. An employee must
        acCompany the non-employee at all times.

    •   Employees may not solicit other employees during work times, except in connection with a Company-
        approved or sponsored event.

    •   Non-employees may not solicit employees or distribute literature of any kind on Company premises.

Violations of this policy should be reported to Human Resources.

                                                                                                          95

Thank You!

  Toolkit Overview:

  Leaders play a critical role in ensuring that change initiatives are successful, but change is difficult
  and involves a distinct process for each person engaged. A focused and organized strategy is
  necessary for the change path to be successful for you, your team, and our company.
  The purpose of this toolkit is to guide leaders through the concepts of change management. It includes
  tools and best practices on how to lead yourself and others through the change management process.
  Who should use this toolkit?
  This toolkit is designed for RealPage leaders and HR Business Partners (HRBP).
  How to use this toolkit?
  The change management process is not linear. It is recommended that you reference the contents of
  this toolkit and use this toolkit throughout your change situation or on an as-needed basis as a guide
  and tool to support yourself and your team during change. Partner with your HRBP for specific
  guidance for your team.
  This toolkit focuses on how leaders can effectively manage Change Management situations and to help
  employees embrace and adopt change in their day-to-day work.
  Content Overview:
  This toolkit is divided into three (3) main parts to help you in any stage of your change situations.
  Part 1: Assessing & Understanding the Change – Helps you learn about the role of a leader in
  navigating and accelerating successful change implementations. You will also be assessing your teams’
  Change IQ to help you better prepare your Change Management approach. You will explore the scope
  of your change situations by exploring the What, Why, When, Who and How of your Change
  situations.
  Part 2: Implementation & Impact: The Change Curve – Helps you understand and be mindful of the
  Emotional Cycle of Change. You will also use different tools to understand and consider the impact of
  Change to People, Process and Technology. You will also think about your Employee & Stakeholder
  Support system and their roles and plan on how to communicate the change effectively.
  Part 3: Reinforcing & Sustaining Change – Helps you think about success metrics that ensures you
  are monitoring the progress and the success of the change. As a leader, it’s critical to be proactive
  and intentional when providing support to your employees when navigating change. You’ll be
  introduced to three-step Mile Markers that will provide best practices and tools to use with your
  teams during each phases of your change.
         Mile Marker:

         1 – Growth Beyond Disruption
         2 – Sustaining Trust
         3 – Create a New Normal

  Change Management
  Change management is the systematic approach to managing employee engagement and adoption
  when an organization changes how work will be done. Its goal is to help individuals and teams adapt to
  changes in the organization in a smooth and efficient manner, while minimizing any obstructive
  impacts that may arise. The vision and details about the change need to be clear, consistent, and
  shared throughout the organization.

  It is important to remember that the change process is not linear. Most change management theories
  visually illustrate the stages of change on a linear curve. In reality, navigating change looks more like
  a roller coaster with many twists and turns. Many times, there is movement forward, followed by
  steps backwards. Processing change depends on the person, the events unfolding, and several other
  factors. The goal is to progress through the change process towards (eventually) acceptance.

  Most online data and publications about change acknowledges that change is difficult, and not all
  change efforts are successful. Without a specific and structured approach, many change efforts
  fall short of the goal, resulting in wasted time, effort, and resources. Taking a focused approach to
  managing change can make the difference between success and failure to meet project goals.

  It’s important to recognize that change does not and will not stop at RealPage. RealPage is going
  through significant “Transformation” but not all change is a Transformation.

  In RealPage there are three categories of change: Run, Improve, Transform

         ▪ Run: Keeping the lights on! These types of change helps maintain current business
           capabilities. These changes help ensure that customers’ expectations are met and
           maintained. Change Timeline – continuously moving forward and is always “today”.

         ▪ Improve: Improve existing business capabilities or employee experience. These changes
           aim for us to get better in what we’re doing and adds value to RealPage (revenue growth,
           renewal, slowing attrition, improve capabilities, etc.). These changes are continuous and
           often focused on improving cost efficiency, productivity, etc.
           Change Timeline – today from the next 3 to 4 years.

         ▪ Transform: Enable new business capabilities. Change that “changes the game” and
           creates new opportunities. Requires rigorous management to be successful.

  It’s important to frame and plan your discussions and change approach based on the needs and
  priorities of your department.

                                                  Internal Use

  Assessing & Understanding the Change
  Assessing and understanding change refers to the process of evaluating a change that an
  organization plans to implement and gaining an understanding of the potential impact of that
  change on the organization, its stakeholders, and its environment.

  I. Leader’s Role

  Leaders play a critical role in change management, as they are responsible for creating and
  communicating a vision for change, guiding the organization through the change process, and
  ensuring that the change is successfully implemented.
  Leaders Accelerate Change: To accelerate the implementation of the change, you’ll need to help
  your team members embrace the change quickly, and in the process, create an agile work
  environment where team members are more open to change.
  There are three main actions, or Change Accelerators that can assist your team in embracing
  change quickly:
        ▪ Describe what’s changing and why: People tend to respond more favorably to change
          when they understand the business reasons for it and can see its benefits.

        ▪ Seek reactions and feelings: Seeking people’s reactions helps them feel heard and
          involved in what’s happening, which can go a long way toward building trust and
          commitment.

        ▪ Regain a sense of control: If people learn that they can control aspects of the change or
          at least have some influence over them, they’ll be more open to change and more likely
          to take steps toward embracing it.

 III. Understanding the Change

 Change is the process of transforming or altering something improve it, adapt it to new circumstances,
 or achieve a specific goal. Change can take many different forms, such as organizational restructuring,

 the objective and scope of the change. This information will serve as a solid foundation for future

  Implementation & Impact

  I. The Change Curve
  Every organization brings about changes in its processes, management, and operations.
  During these changes, there must be a change in the people as well. Only when people make
  the transitions can the organization move ahead and reap the full benefits of the change.
  The quicker teammates move along on their journey through the cycle of change, the easier it will
  be for our organization to move towards success. The change curve can help you better
  understand and anticipate how one will react to change and how to provide support to your team
  members.
  The emotional cycle of change model was created by Don Kelly and Daryl Conner. The cycle
  shows five stages – Uninformed Optimism, Informed Pessimism, Valley of Despair, Informed
  Optimism, and Fulfillment. This outlines how your emotional response (usually based on how
  much the change will affect you personally) is likely to alter as you go through a change.
  In this emotional cycle of change, people can easily get into the valley of despair. It's important to
  acknowledge that this is part of the change process, and you need to help your team members
  move through this stage as quickly as possible. The change continuum below the change
  curve shows the behaviors of these stages of emotions: Resisting, Observing, Accommodating and
  Embracing.
  The change curve is not linear, but the goal is to move towards the future, eventually to embrace the
  change as a new norm.

  Identify your Change Champion, Change Agents and Change Empath

  Change Champions

  Role: Participate in the planning of change management. Helps in implementing and promoting the change. Provide
  ideas and solutions to address change process gaps.

  Change Agents

  Characteristics: These employees adapt to new initiatives and are able to quickly see the benefits of change and are
  willing to embrace change. They are willing to take on new challenges, learn new skills, and help to create a culture
  that is innovative and growth oriented.

  Role: Observes and monitors the change, provides feedback about the effect, impact and benefits of the change
  throughout the change implementation, helps in creating a change culture behavior in the team.

  Change Empaths
  Characteristics: These employees have the ability to sense and observe people’s feeling and reactions. They help
  create a positive environment. They are easily trusted and relied on by their teammates.

  Role: Touchbase with the team to learn and understand the personal effect of change for team members. Support
  team members during the change implementation process. Provide feedback, ideas, and solutions that

 Communication Plan Considerations
 Communication is critical when it comes to Change Management! The goal of change
 communication is to facilitate sustained realization of the change goal by recommitting
 people along the way. As you are communicating change, keep in mind that people have a
 limited capacity to absorb information under stress, so you need to be consistent and
 purposeful in your communication. Communicate often and frequently.
 Consider the following when planning your communication:
        ▪ Communication Objectives: Think about what you want to achieve before making
          any communication actions. Your objectives should align with the change vision and
          business objective.

        ▪ Desired Behavior: As you draft the words in your communication think about the
          change in mindset and behaviors that you want to achieve in your message. What
          do you want your audience to feel about the message and the change? How do you
          want your audience to react?

        ▪ Modes of Communication: Communication is not a one-size fits all. Think about
          your audience and teams and plan the best avenue for communication. Do you
          need to set up meetings (small-large), send emails, create a group chat, have 1:1
          discussions, etc.

        ▪ Communication Content: Each communication should be intentionally planned.
          Think about the relevant and useful information that you put in your
          communication content that will help you achieve your objectives like updates,
          resources, key milestones, acknowledgement, calls to action items, data or results
          and celebrations.

        ▪ Communication Cadence: The frequency of communication and timelines should
          be closely tied to your change management plans and should reflect intermittent
          milestones that celebrate success.

        ▪ Communication Calendar: This will layout the what and when the
          communication will need to happen from beginning to the end of Change
          Management Implementation.

  II. Mile Markers
  One of the most impactful ways to lead your team through change is to model the behavior
  that you want to see in them. With many teammates working in a hybrid environment, it’s
  critical to be proactive and intentional with the support you provide. To navigate the change, the
  following three-step Road Map provides best practices and tools to use with your teams during each
  phase.
               Mile Marker:
                   1. Growth Beyond Disruption
                   2. Sustaining Trust
                   3. Create a New Normal
  These Mile Markers indicate the direction we are heading. You may determine to use the tools in
  sequential order, while other leaders will use them differently. These tools are available for you to
  leverage, as needed, depending on what is happening, specific to you and your team. The overall goal is
  to lead your team through the transition of past to future.

  Mile Marker 1 – Growth Beyond Disruption
  When to use: Most useful when a new change is announced and there is disruption happening. Many
  people will have the tendency to resist or observe the change at this point. Often these reactions
  occur because of the uncertainty of what the future holds.

  BEST PRACTICES

          ▪ Sleep on it. Refrain from sharing your thoughts, feelings, and reactions just yet.
          ▪ Evaluate by yourself or with others what aspects of the change you can control or
            influence and what aspects you can’t control.
          ▪ Seek to understand the vision and the change strategy. Post this information in your
            work areas or on your team intranet site.
          ▪ Don’t jump to conclusions or make assumptions. Instead, make a list of clarifying
            questions.
          ▪ Determine how the change differs from your expectations: “I expected _____; now,
            _____ might happen.”
          ▪ Ask yourself, “How does this change affect my plans for the future?” Make a list of what
            you will gain or lose.
          ▪ Consider the business impact of the change. Ask yourself, “What good could come of this
            change in terms of budget, resources, time, profitability, productivity, morale,
            customers, and competition?”
          ▪ Know that you can and will get through this change. Say a daily affirmation.
          ▪ Ask yourself, “What is it about this change that is making me feel fearful, anxious, excited,
            etc.?”
          ▪ Apply lessons learned from similar change experiences.
          ▪ Periodically revisit your Change IQ. Consciously reframe your thoughts to enhance your
            placement.
          ▪ Identify what you need before you can move to the next phase of change. Think about
            what is feasible and what resources you need to make it happen.

  Mile Marker 2 – Sustaining Trust
  At this point, more information is known, and people are beginning to understand the circumstances
  better. This is a critical time to maintain and sustain trust with your team.

  BEST PRACTICES

          ▪ Seek information from your business world—team members, leadership, competition,
            customers, technologies, regulations.
          ▪ Develop a network of people with whom you can discuss lessons learned, fears,
            challenges, expectations, strategies, and progress.
          ▪ Be a catalyst by supporting and encouraging others to enhance their Change IQs.
            Use Key Principles.
          ▪ Create a community bulletin board or intranet site to discuss issues, generate ideas,
            and track progress toward the change.
          ▪ Identify barriers and solicit support from appropriate resources.
          ▪ List the positives and negatives of the change during a team meeting. Revisit the list
            periodically; record insights about the benefits and brainstorm strategies to overcome the
            challenges.
          ▪ Make discussion of rumors and assumptions a standing agenda item for team meetings.
          ▪ Clarify roles, responsibilities, and degree of ownership with leaders.
          ▪ Ask yourself and others, “Are we getting in the way of our own success by being satisfied
            with the status quo or not being open to change?”
          ▪ Commit to being part of the implementation, then identify and set ambitious goals.
          ▪ Determine quick steps to build momentum toward the change goal. When
            identifying these steps, ask yourself and others, “Will this activity increase
            productivity?”
          ▪ Work with others to make the change work. Eliminate wasteful or obsolete activities.
          ▪ Don’t be satisfied with initial ideas—push yourself and others to generate other
            options before committing to a course of action.
          ▪ Think creatively to identify helpful resources.
          ▪ Generate a list of questions, such as, “What are our roles and responsibilities? What
            level of decision-making will we have?” and then ask them of the appropriate people.
            Understand that answers to all your questions might not be available right away.
          ▪ Identify short-term goals, track progress, and then celebrate short-term wins.
          ▪ Ask yourself, “What can I do to make this change work?” List all the possibilities.
          ▪ Identify information-gathering activities, such as Internet searches, webinars, or
            interviews, that you can do to move closer to the change goal.
          ▪ Take action with urgency and purpose. Make strides toward the change goal every day.
            Identify specific dates for getting things done.
          ▪ Identify opportunities to work with people who are positive, supportive, or
            enthusiastic about this change. Watch, listen, and apply lessons learned.
          ▪ Find out what people are doing to succeed in other organizations undergoing change.
            Consider how their methods could be applied to your organization.

Lead to Exceed
Manager Guide

             For RealPage Internal Use Only

                                           Internal Use

                       Lead to Exceed Manager Guide

One or more of your direct reports is/are participating in RealPage’s six-week development
program for manager to director levels, Lead to Exceed. As the participant's manager, you
play a critical role in ensuring results from their learning and development activities. This
guide will help you support and reinforce the lessons from the Lead to Exceed.

This Manager Guide is organized as follows:

Program Overview
▪ Explains overall program structure and course roadmap to provide you with a preview of
  what your employee will experience in and outside the classroom.

Before the Session
▪ Provides an action list of what you can do to ensure participants arrive at the session
  prepared and motivated.

Overview of Course Content
▪ Presents key course content to help you understand and reinforce the use of the
  concepts, skills, and techniques introduced in the course.

After the Session: Reinforcing and Supporting Application
▪ Provides an action list you may refer to and use at any time to help participants
  successfully apply what they’ve learned on their job.
▪ Development planning with the participant after the session

                                 For RealPage Internal Use Only

                                                      Internal Use

Program Overview
Lead to Exceed is designed to provide RealPage leaders (manager to director levels) with
essential leadership skills to drive performance and results. It is also a prerequisite for
higher leadership development programs.

The program is divided into three sessions: Leading Self, Leading Others and Leading the
Business. It uses a combination of learning methodologies including self-paced pre-work,
micro-courses or e-Learning, and learning group discussions to ensure networking and
peer-to-peer coaching.

Session Roadmap

    Manager Orientation, Participant    Pre-work: Self-Paced – 40 min               Pre-work: Self-Paced – 40 min
    Welcome Email & pre-work sent out   • SMART Goals                               • Driving Change
    in advance                          • Building an Inclusive Culture
                                                                                    Live: Virtual Classroom – 2.5 hrs
    • Kick-off Session – 60 min         Live: Virtual Classroom – 2.5 hrs           • Executing Strategy at the Front
                                        • Coaching: Move People Forward                Line
    Pre-work: Self-Paced – 40 min                                                   • Graduation

    Live: Virtual Classroom – 2.5 hrs

       Management
    • Leading Self: Turn Awareness                                                  Overall Course Evaluation
       into Impact
                                                                                    Development Plan Conversation
    Post-work: Microcourse – 7-20min:                                               with Leader
    • Embracing Change: Yourself &
      Others

    Learning Group Discussion: 1 hr.

                                             Total Time Investment: 14.5 hours
                                                     Self-Paced: 2 hours
                                          Live Group Virtual Classroom: 8.5 hours

Before the Session
Help the participants come to the sessions prepared and motivated.

▪ Encourage participants to complete all required pre-work.
▪ Provide the time and resources needed for participants to attend each session in its
  entirety.
▪ Listen for and openly discuss resistance to attend a session. Work with your leaders to
  find ways to overcome barriers.
▪ Schedule a meeting with each person to be held immediately after training, if possible,
  to follow up and discuss how the person will apply what they learned.

                                        For RealPage Internal Use Only

                                              Internal Use

Overview of Course Content

Session 1: Leading Self
Weeks 1-2
Pre-Work

Communication: Connect Through Conversations

Overview

Leaders work eight hours, often more, every day. During that time, they face the challenge of
communicating and connecting with the people they lead through conversations that usually
focus on business goals. Good leaders also use these as opportunities to acknowledge
people’s feelings and concerns by connecting on a deeper level. Communication: Connect
Through Conversations explores that deeper connection, the head and heart—the whole
person—and helps participants gain insights and learn techniques and skills to increase their
confidence in successfully navigating those “in the moment” conversations, even the tough
ones.

In this course, participants will learn to:

       ▪ Conduct conversations that achieve their intended business goals.
       ▪ Communicate and respond in ways that meet the unique personal needs of team
         members and others.
       ▪ Recognize and react to emotions (theirs and others’) present in work situations.
       ▪ Use a technique to provide meaningful, and supportive feedback

Communicating with Head and Heart

Through two tools, learners gain insight into how well they recognize their own emotions as
well as the emotions that others express. They recognize that they can improve their
emotional intelligence through the application of a powerful set of communication skills, and
this can have a strong impact on their success as a leader.

Interaction Essentials
The Interaction Essentials comprise two sets of communication
skills: Key Principles and Interaction Guidelines.
Key Principles address the heart and meet people’s personal need to feel valued and
respected in interactions. They are:
       •    Maintain or enhance self-esteem.
       •    Listen and respond with empathy.
       •    Ask for help and encourage involvement.
       •    Share thoughts, feelings, and rationale. (to build trust)
       •    Provide support without removing responsibility. (to build ownership)

                                    For RealPage Internal Use Only

                                          Internal Use

Interaction Guidelines—Open, Clarify, Develop, Agree, and Close—provide a structure
that ensures leaders engage the head and achieve the business goals—that is, the practical
needs that are the reason for the conversation.
STAR and STAR/AR Feedback
Participants learn about STAR, an approach to giving complete and specific feedback
that reminds the leader to describe:
       ▪ ST—Situation or Task. What was the problem, business opportunity, challenge,
         or task?
       ▪ A—Action. What was said or done to handle or respond to the situation or
         task?
       ▪ R—Result. What happened, for better or worse, because of the person’s or
         team’s actions, and what was the impact or consequence of that result?
       An additional AR component for providing developmental feedback includes:
       ▪ An Alternative Action—something the person or team could have said or done
         differently.
       ▪ The enhanced Result that the alternative action might have produced.

Live Virtual Class
Transition to Management
According to Harvard Business School’s extensive research on career transitions, making
the leap from individual contributor to people manager counts among the most challenging
transitions in business life. People often move into a new role and start “doing” without
investing the time to learn about the new role. Many managers fail because they do not
recognize the transition that must occur as they shift their roles. They move forward doing
what they do best—delivering excellent individual contributor work.
In this session, participants learn about the nine mistakes new people managers often make
and discuss ways to overcome them.

                                For RealPage Internal Use Only

                                              Internal Use

Turn Awareness into Impact
Overview
A more accurate self-perception has long been a predictor of success in life and as a
leader. Self-awareness arms leaders with knowledge that enables them to make better
decisions, build stronger relationships, and know which of their qualities to leverage and
which to mitigate. On the other hand, a lack of self-awareness can be an obstacle to the
growth of a leader. This course helps leaders to gain insights to more intentionally be
their best selves.
In this course participants will:
▪ Increase internal self-awareness by identifying their emotions, talents and aligning
  their values with those of RealPage’s.
▪ Identify their emotional triggers and learn tactics to manage their response.
▪ Identify their leadership talents to leverage for greater positive impact.

Internal Self-Awareness Model

The internal self-awareness model is explained through the analogy of
a tree:
▪ Values are shown as the roots because they are the foundation of
  people’s behavior, actions, and decisions.
▪ Emotions are the trunk—where the heart is.
▪ Branches represent talents because they can grow and multiply
  over time. The course provides activities, content, and guidance to
  explore these three areas.

Values
Learners will review RealPage’s Core Values. Participants will identify a core value that
resonates with them the most and share ways they can advocate it within their teams.

Emotions

With emotional intelligence positioned as a key factor in a
leader’s success, learners explore the emotional triggers that
can lead them to react with unwanted or inappropriate
behavior.
In a variety of activities, participants discuss and share
response management tactics for controlling their immediate
reactions when triggered. With coaching from their peers,
learners develop a self-directive—a plan for what they’ll do
differently when triggered to avoid behavior they might later
regret.

                                    For RealPage Internal Use Only

                                           Internal Use

Talents
Before the session, learners complete a self-insight tool that
helps them see where their most natural talents lie in a model
of six core leadership talents. Learners explore the six talents
in greater depth and then identify the talents they rated
highest and most energizing for themselves.

They recognize how awareness of their talents can enhance their impact as a leader. In a
small group activity, learners get coaching on a workplace challenge from peers who are
stronger in different talents and thus gain the benefit of their diverse perspectives.
Learners commit to take one action related to applying their talents.

Post-Work Micro-course: Embracing Change – Yourself and Others
Change is universal. However, it manifests itself in very different ways depending on the
situation, the environment, the people, and the timing.
This course will help participants:
▪ Discover their position in the Change IQ Continuum.
▪ Learn the three phases' people go through before they can embrace change.

Three Phases of Change

▪ Disorientation – people feel confused, anxious, uncertain or concerned about the
  change.
▪ Reorientation – people make discoveries, learn and begin to feel greater sense of
  control over their situation.
▪ Integration – people adjust. What was once unsettling is now normal. The change has
  become part of the routine. They are in the final phase before fully embracing change.

                                 For RealPage Internal Use Only

                                            Internal Use

Session 2: Leading Others
Weeks 3-4

Pre-Work
SMART Goals
Overview
A successful performance process starts with setting clear and achievable goals. When
team members are in control of their work processes and outcomes, they are more
engaged and strive for better results.
This course will help participants to shift from the traditional approach of command
leadership and engage their team members to share responsibility for their performance.
They will learn to:

▪   Demonstrate shared ownership for setting goals, gathering data, tracking progress, and
    reviewing results.
▪   Compose performance goals that are specific, measurable, attainable, relevant, and
    time bound.
▪   Evaluate how team members are accomplishing their goals based on performance data.
▪   Use essential interaction skills to meet personal and practical needs during
    performance discussions.
▪   Provide ongoing coaching and feedback throughout the performance cycle.

Introduction

Leaders are introduced to a model which depicts shared
ownership for managing performance and the roles and
responsibilities of each person throughout an entire performance
cycle.

At the start of the cycle, leaders and direct reports work together
to set goals, and then review results during the cycle. While the
leader provides ongoing coaching on the direct report’s
performance, both are responsible for tracking progress and
sharing feedback.

                                  For RealPage Internal Use Only

                                              Internal Use

SMART Performance Goals
Leaders learn how to write effective performance goals using the SMART criteria:
▪ Specific—defines specific results to be achieved.
▪ Measurable—defines quantity, cost, or quality metrics to determine progress.
▪ Attainable—allows the goal to be challenging, yet the person can still ensure results.
▪ Relevant—supports the achievement of team or organizational goals.
▪ Time bound—specifies a due date, time frame, or frequency rate.

Gathering Data
Learners are introduced to two types of data they need to gather to track their direct
reports’ performance—operational and behavioral:
▪ Operational data provides information on direct reports’ progress on what they are
  expected to achieve (their SMART goals). This type of data can come from sources such
  as calendars, project timelines, reports, and feedback surveys.
▪ Behavioral data provides information on how direct reports are accomplishing their
  goals. This type of data can be tracked by gathering feedback from direct reports and
  others in the form of a STAR (Situation/Task, Action, Result).
Reviewing Results
The Interaction Essentials—Interaction Guidelines and Key Principles—are skills your
leaders learned in the Leading Self module to help them meet personal and practical needs
during discussions. While all Interaction Essentials are valuable, some are more helpful
when setting goals and when reviewing results.

Live Virtual Class
Coaching: Move People Forward
Overview
The need to coach can happen at any time. In these moments, leaders should have a go-to
approach for coming alongside people and helping them achieve a goal. This course shows
leaders how to move people forward by creating a relationship built on trust, meeting their
personal and practical needs right where they are, and energizing them into action.
In this course, participants will learn to:
       ▪ Recognize and nurture the potential within others to grow and change.
       ▪ Flex their approach to meet the unique needs of each person, whether they’re
         coaching for success or for improvement.
       ▪ Guide, inspire, support, and empower in the moment.
       ▪ Ask questions, connect at a human level, and energize into action.

                                   For RealPage Internal Use Only

                                            Internal Use

Insights and the Impact of Coaching
Coaches do make an impact—good or bad. To have a positive impact, leaders must approach
coaching with the mindset that people can grow and change. They also must be willing to
open and disclose thoughts, feelings, and rationale to build the trust that’s needed in a good
coaching relationship. Through self-insight tools, learners explore where their tendencies
lie in these areas and how they can adjust their words and actions to coach more effectively.

Ask, Connect, Energize

Whether coaching happens in the moment or is planned, there’s an
easy-to-remember approach: Ask, Connect, and Energize (ACE).

▪ Ask is about asking questions to clarify details and involve people in thinking things
  through on their own.
▪ Connect is about leaning in and cultivating trust through empathy and sharing to
  better understand where people are coming from.
▪ Energize is about building ownership with your support and igniting confidence with
  esteem. Learners practice ACE through a variety of engaging activities that challenge
  them on what they would say and do to use each technique.

Coaching Conversation Skills
Sometimes coaching is more involved and requires planning:
That’s where the Interaction Essentials come in. These two sets
of communication skills—Interaction Guidelines and Key
Principles—provide structure to a conversation.

Interaction Guidelines
Open, Clarify, Develop, Agree, Close
Key Principles Open - the personal "human" needs that people have
Esteem, Empathy, Involvement, Share, Support

Post-Work Micro-course:
Developing Individual Team Members
Overview
Development is a shared responsibility between both the leader and the person being
developed. In this microcourse, participants will learn that successful development involves
three phases – assessing development goals, determining ways to acquire learning, and
providing opportunities to apply the learning on the job.

                                  For RealPage Internal Use Only

                                            Internal Use

Session 3: Leading the Business
Weeks 4-6

Self-Paced Pre-Work
Driving Change
Overview
Resistance to change is a normal reaction, even when it will ultimately benefit an employee,
their teams, and the organization.
Successfully completing Driving Change will enable learners to:
▪   Prepare to effectively communicate the business rationale for change.
▪   Use three actions to accelerate implementation.
▪   Recognize the nature of resistance and use a set of skills to respond to it.
▪   Determine aspects of the change that can be controlled.
▪   Use essential interaction skills to conduct effective discussions to move closer to
    embracing change.

Change Accelerators
Participants are introduced to three Change Accelerators they can
use to implement change more quickly for their own change
situation:
▪ Describe what’s changing and why. Explaining the business reasons for and expected
  benefits of the change helps people understand and accept it.
▪ Seek reactions and feelings. Drawing out and then responding to people’s concerns
  can move them past any emotional barriers that are holding them back.
▪ Regain a sense of control. Learning that they can control or at least influence aspects
  of the change can help people begin to accept it more quickly.

Change Reactions Continuum
It’s important to recognize people’s reactions to change and respond in a way that helps
them move forward. In this micro course, learners explore four common reactions and
determine where their team members are on the continuum.

Personal and Practical Needs of Change

Participants learn how to use the Interaction Essentials —Key Principles and Interaction
Guidelines—to meet the personal and practical needs of individuals during change.

                                  For RealPage Internal Use Only

                                           Internal Use

Live Session
Executing Strategy at the Frontline
Overview
▪ Communicate how their priorities align with the organization’s strategic goals.
▪ Focus their and their team’s time, attention, and energy on the highest priorities.
▪ Determine how to track progress and assess outcomes for each priority.
▪ Apply best practices to hold people accountable for the work they’ve assigned them.

Participants are introduced to three elements of strategy execution:
▪ Focus
▪ Measurement
▪ Accountability
The majority of activities in the session guide participants to explore these elements
within the context of their own top priorities; thus, the benefits are specific to each
person. The Strategy Execution Tool helps leaders visualize and assess the status of top
priorities, related measurements, and accountable individuals.

Focus
Put critical priorities first.
When a leader and his or her team are focused, they consistently take actions and invest
time and energy on the critical priorities that contribute to accomplishing the
organization’s goals. They recover quickly from distractions while balancing daily
operational needs, customer demands, and financial requirements.
▪ Focus is prioritizing a few important things and communicating these items to the team.
▪ These priorities get more attention, more review, and more discussion because they’re
  the most critical for success.

Measurement
Track progress and assess outcomes.
Leaders cannot manage what they don’t measure. It’s important to establish both progress
and outcome measures for key priorities:
▪ Progress measures and monitors trends that can enable leaders to predict their ability
  to reach a goal or objective.
▪ Outcome measures describe what success will look like. They measure what has been
  achieved after the fact compared to the desired outcome.

                                 For RealPage Internal Use Only

                                            Internal Use

Adhering to the following criteria will ensure that metrics will be sound:
Objective: from a perspective that people can agree on.
▪ Actionable; yielding information that people can act on.
▪ Consistently trackable over time.
▪ Easy to implement; readily available.
▪ Quantifiable; stated as a number or percentage.
▪ Relevant; yielding information to reveal trends, progress, and barriers.

Accountability
Assign work and reinforce responsibility.
Leaders often struggle with enforcing accountability. They are responsible for holding
people accountable in appropriate ways, ensuring that the right people do the right things
at the right times.
Four accountability best practices are:
▪ Hold one person accountable for each progress measure. Leaders should avoid “joint
  accountability,” which leads to inaction or confusion. (However, in some cases it is
  appropriate for multiple team members to have an identical individual measure, such as a
  quota or rate.)
▪ Communicate accountability, including consequences. A leader needs to discuss
  expectations with each person, including the consequences if the work exceeds or falls
  short of the measures outlined.
▪ Set monitoring and/or follow-up methods. The leader should discuss with each person
  the ways in which the work will be monitored and clarify the expectation that he or she
  will follow up regularly. The leader also should encourage people to speak up when
  obstacles arise.
▪ Offer feedback and coaching. The leader should reassure each team member that they
  will provide feedback and coaching to help ensure the person is successful.

                                  For RealPage Internal Use Only

                                             Internal Use

Post-work Micro-course:
Letting Go and Delegating More
Overview
In this microcourse, learners will learn the benefits of delegation to oneself, their team and
the organization. They will also discover how to deal with their own hesitations to delegating
and the learn some best practices to delegating effectively.

After the Session: Reinforcing and Supporting Application
Reinforce and support your team member’s application of skills in the workplace.
▪ Encourage Accountability. Hold participants accountable for consciously using the
  Interaction Essentials to meet personal and practical needs in their interactions.
▪ Offer Support. Discuss your direct report’s application plan and offer your support in
  implementing their plans.
▪ Measure Progress. Work with people to identify and agree on ways to measure their
  progress and success in applying their newly learned skills and knowledge.
▪ Use Collaboration Tools. Take advantage of technology to sustain learning and
  development. For example, share links to articles, videos, and other online tools that
  reinforce the importance and impact of providing and responding to effective feedback.
▪ Address Barriers. Discuss barriers that are preventing people from applying new skills
  and help them plan how to overcome them.
▪ Follow Up. Schedule a meeting immediately after training, if possible, to follow up on how
  the person will apply what they learned. Regularly check in on formal or informal
  discussions to ensure people are applying the new skills and that their use of them is
  positively affecting performance. Then, incorporate feedback on their skills in their
  performance reviews.
▪ Recognize Successes. As participants begin to consciously apply what they learned,
  acknowledge and appreciate the impact—big or small—their work is having on business
  success.

                                   For RealPage Internal Use Only

                                            Internal Use

After the Session: Reinforcing and Supporting Application
Reinforce and support your team member’s application of skills in the workplace.
Development Planning
To further support the learners’ career growth and development, the participant will be
asked to complete a Development Plan and will set up a meeting to review the development
plan with you.
The following questions can help you throughout the conversation:
▪ Why is this development goal important?
▪ How will you accomplish the developmental goal? Identify specific behaviors,
  experiences, projects, assignments, or deliverables to achieve this objective.
▪ What resources and/or support do you need to accomplish the developmental goal
  (i.e., time/money/tools/equipment/people)?
▪ How can I help you with this development goal?

                           For any questions, please email:
                        LearningDevelopment@realpage.com

  Program Overview:

  Our RealPage leaders hold great importance in helping ensure that employees are guided
  and supported to deliver exceptional results. Effective leaders are able to coach, develop
  their team members, and share their thoughts and ideas on what works well and what
  needs improvement, all while managing day-to-day tasks.

  The Learn to Lead program is designed with the RealPage Core Values, Purpose, and
  leadership competencies. It aims to develop participants with the skills and knowledge
  required to successfully lead teams, drive results, and foster a culture of continuous
  improvement.

  The Learn to Lead program is crafted to empower and enable leaders to make a positive
  impact on RealPage’s culture and success.

    foster an inclusive environment.
